idiom_name: single visit method with case/when class dispatch and an explicit unsupported branch
implementation_notes: Ruby has no method overloading or static interface set, so the simplest selective visitor is one visit(node) method with case/when branches and an explicit else; Class#=== matches subclasses in branch order. An arbitrary visitor object can instead expose optional per-node hooks selected with respond_to?, but that is duck typing rather than a type-checked acyclic interface family. The bundled RBS gem's RBS::AST::Visitor is a real class-based visitor with a case dispatcher and visit_* hooks, illustrating the conventional Ruby alternative. Use modules or open classes when behavior belongs naturally to the node; keep a visitor when the operation needs a separately replaceable object.
code_sketch:
class AreaVisitor
  attr_reader :area

  def initialize
    @area = 0.0
  end

  def visit(node)
    case node
    when Circle then @area += Math::PI * node.radius ** 2
    when Rect   then @area += node.width * node.height
    else
      warn "no handler for #{node.class}"
    end
  end
end
pitfalls: case/when uses Class#=== so it matches subclasses in the order the branches are written; putting a base class before a derived one makes the derived branch unreachable.
There is no compile-time coverage: a new node type falls into the else branch, and if no else branch exists the visit silently does nothing.
Metaprogrammed dispatch via send("visit_#{node.class}") breaks on namespaced classes (the interpolated name contains ::) and on renamed constants, so prefer explicit branches or a lookup table.
